en: The Perfection of Wisdom in Five Hundred Lines.
Homage to the Blessed Noble Perfection of Wisdom!
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great community of monks and a great host of bodhisattvas.
There, the Blessed One addressed Subhūti.

Subhūti, form is non-existence, yet it is not non-existence; it is existence. Subhūti, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existence, yet they are not non-existence; they are existence. The eye and forms, and eye-consciousness; the ear and sounds, and ear-consciousness; the nose and odors, and nose-consciousness; the tongue and tastes, and tongue-consciousness; the body and tangibles, and body-consciousness...
Subhūti, knowledge, the mind, mental phenomena, and mental consciousness are neither non-existence nor existence; they are true existence.
Thus, those foolish ordinary persons, not understanding that form as it truly is through its threefold revolution, become attached to that form, bring it into being,
and veil it. Being attached to, bringing into being, and veiling that form, they [proceed] by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha...
They will not attain deliverance even by means of the vehicle of the disciples, let alone by the Mahāyāna.
Clinging in such a manner, bringing [existence] about, and obscuring [the truth], they experience old age and death for a long time. That which...
And also among the denizens of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans.
In the same way, Subhūti, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither non-existence nor existence; they are being.
So too are the eye and forms, eye-consciousness;
the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness; the nose and odors, nose-consciousness.

The tongue, tastes, tongue-consciousness; the body, tangibles, body-consciousness; and the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness, Subhūti, are neither non-existence nor existence, but are true existence.
Thus, regarding that mind-consciousness, foolish ordinary people—failing to understand it as it truly is through its threefold revolution—cling to it, bring it into being, and conceal it.
Adhering to that consciousness, bringing it forth, and concealing [the truth],
they will not go forth by means of either the Śrāvaka-vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle,
let alone by the Mahāyāna.
Adhering in this way,
bringing [it] forth, and concealing [it], they experience old age and death for a long time.
Namely, among hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans.

And thus, when the wise understand that form as it truly is through its threefold revolution, they do not adhere to it, they do not bring it about, and they reveal it. Not adhering to it, not bringing it about, and revealing it, they set forth by means of the Mahāyāna.
What need is there to mention the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle?
Thus, not being attached and not bringing about rebirth while elucidating [the truth], they do not experience old age and death.
Namely, among hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans.

In this way, by means of the three turnings, the wise, understanding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are, do not adhere to them, do not bring them about, and illuminate them.
Not adhering [to anything], not bringing [anything] into existence, and elucidating it by means of the Mahāyāna, they thus go forth;
what need is there to mention [those who do so] by means of the Śrāvakayāna or the Pratyekabuddhayāna?
And thus, not adhering, not bringing into existence, and elucidating, they are not subject to old age—(3)
They experience death,
namely, in the hells, among animals, among hungry ghosts, among gods, and among humans.
Subhūti, form arises and ceases.
That which is the arising of form is its non-arising;
that which is the arising of form is its nature of non-arising.
Regarding form:
for a bodhisattva who understands, as it truly is, that very nature of non-arising of form, that non-arising of form is accomplished.
In the same way, Subhūti, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness arise and pass away.
That which is the arising of consciousness is its non-arising;
that which is the nature of the non-arising of the arising of consciousness is the nature of consciousness.
Furthermore, for a bodhisattva who understands that very nature of non-arising of consciousness as it truly is, that non-arising of consciousness is accomplished.
Subhūti, whoever should say that form is the self or belongs to the self, I declare him to be an outsider, one who stands on the side of ordinary worldlings, and one possessed of false views.

Subhūti, whoever should say that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are the self or belong to the self— I call such a person an outsider, one who stands on the side of the common folk, and one possessed of false views.

Subhūti, whoever should say that form has as its cause what was previously done, or has as its cause the creation of Īśvara, or is without cause and conditions— I call him an outsider, one who stands on the side of ordinary worldlings, and one possessed of false views.
Subhūti, whoever should say that feeling, perception, mental formations,

or consciousness have as their cause what was previously done, or have as their cause the creation of Īśvara, or are without cause and conditions— I call such a person an outsider, one who stands on the side of ordinary worldlings, and one possessed of false views.

Subhūti, if anyone were to say that form has the characteristic of deformation, feeling has the characteristic of experiencing, perception has the characteristic of perceiving, mental formations have the characteristic of volitional construction, and consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing—
I would call such a person an outsider among outsiders, one who stands on the side of ordinary worldlings, and one possessed of false views.

Subhūti, whoever should say, "Form is suffering and unpeaceful; the cessation of form is happiness and peace," even him I call one who is external, more external than the external, one who stands on the side of the ordinary worldlings, and one who holds false views.

Subhūti, whoever should say, "Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering and unpeaceful; the cessation of consciousness is happiness and peace," I call him an outsider beyond the outsiders, one who stands on the side of ordinary worldlings, and one possessed of false views.

Subhūti, even he who should say, "Form indeed does not exist," I declare him to be more external than the external, one who stands on the side of the common worldlings, and one possessed of false views.

Subhūti, whoever should say, "Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist at all," I declare that person to be outside even of the external, one who stands on the side of ordinary worldlings and possesses false views.

Subhūti, if anyone were to say: "That which was taught by the Blessed One regarding the lack of intrinsic nature of form— that it is unarisen, unceasing, originally quiescent, and naturally parinirvāṇized— all that teaching is without intentional meaning, without underlying purpose, and should be understood exactly according to the literal expression," I would call such a person an outsider beyond the pale, one who stands on the side of the common worldlings, and one possessed of false views.

Subhūti, whoever should say: "That which was taught by the Blessed One regarding the lack of intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— namely, that they are unarisen, unceasing, primordially peaceful, and naturally in a state of parinirvāṇa—

all that teaching is without intentional meaning, without underlying purpose, and should be understood exactly according to the literal expression," I declare that person to be external, even more external, standing on the side of ordinary worldlings, and possessed of false views.
Subhūti, there is form which leads to non-attachment to form, to its non-arising, and to its non-conceptualization;
there is that form which leads to the defilement of form,
to its reliance, and to its entry.
There exists that form which leads to the purification and realization of form.
Subhūti, there is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness which lead to non-attachment to consciousness, to its non-arising, and to its non-discrimination.
Subhūti, there is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness which lead to the defilement of consciousness, to its reliance, and to its entry [into further existence].
There is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness which lead to the purification and mastery of consciousness.
(7) Subhūti, there is form which, having been abandoned and fully understood by Bodhisattvas, leads to mastery through teaching.
Subhūti, there is form which, having been abandoned and fully understood, leads to mastery through demonstration.
Subhūti, there exists form which, when abandoned and fully understood, conduces to the possession of white dharmas, to mastery over dharmas, and to dwelling in great bliss.

Subhūti, there are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness which, when abandoned and fully understood by Bodhisattvas, lead to their teaching and mastery. Subhūti, there are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness which, when abandoned and fully understood, lead to their manifestation and mastery.

Subhūti, there exist feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness which, when abandoned and fully understood by Bodhisattvas, lead to the possession of pure qualities, to mastery over all phenomena, and to dwelling in great bliss.
Subhūti, any bodhisattva who does not perceive form as merely form and merely suffering perceives a self in form.
He who perceives a self in form perceives a view of self in form.
He who perceives a view of self in form perceives everything in form.
He who perceives everything in form does not perceive anything in form.
He who, while perceiving everything in form, does not perceive anything— that perception of his becomes perfected.
Relying on that apprehension, he does not even depart by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
let alone by means of the Mahāyāna.
Subhūti, any bodhisattva who does not perceive in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that there is merely consciousness or merely suffering, perceives a self in consciousness.
Whoever perceives a self in consciousness perceives a view of self in consciousness.
Whoever perceives a view of self in consciousness perceives everything in consciousness.
He who perceives everything within consciousness does not perceive anything within consciousness.
He who, while perceiving everything within consciousness, does not perceive anything—that perception of his becomes perfected.
Relying upon that perception, he does not yet depart by means of either the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
How much more so, then, by means of the Mahāyāna!
Furthermore, Subhūti, he who perceives in form merely form and merely suffering does not apprehend a self in form.
He who does not apprehend a self in form does not apprehend the view of a self in form.
He who does not perceive a self-view regarding form does not perceive anything regarding form. He who does not perceive anything regarding form perceives everything regarding form.
For him who, not perceiving anything regarding form, perceives everything, that perception of his becomes perfected.
Relying upon that apprehension, he goes forth by means of either the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, but not by means of the Mahāyāna. (9)
Furthermore, Subhūti, whoever perceives in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that there is only consciousness and only suffering, does not apprehend a self in consciousness.
Whoever does not apprehend a self in consciousness does not apprehend a view of self in consciousness.
Whoever does not apprehend a view of self in consciousness does not apprehend anything at all in consciousness.
He who does not perceive anything in consciousness perceives everything in consciousness;
he who [perceives] everything in consciousness...
Not perceiving anything, he perceives everything; that constitutes his perfected perception.
Relying upon that perception, he goes forth by means of either the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, but not by means of the Mahāyāna.
Subhūti, whoever does not perceive form as being merely an unreal mental construction and merely an error, he perceives form within form.
Whoever [perceives] form within form...
He who perceives form perceives the view of form;
he who perceives the view of form perceives everything in form.
He who perceives everything in form does not perceive anything in form.
He who, while perceiving everything in form, does not perceive anything—that perception of his is perfected.
Relying upon that perception, he does not yet depart by means of either the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
How much more so, then, by means of the Mahāyāna!
Subhūti, whoever does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being merely unreal imagination and mere delusion, he perceives consciousness within consciousness.
Whoever perceives consciousness within consciousness perceives a view of consciousness within consciousness;
whoever perceives a view of consciousness within consciousness perceives everything within consciousness.
He who perceives everything in consciousness does not perceive anything in consciousness;
he who, while perceiving everything in consciousness, does not perceive anything— that perception of his is perfected.
Relying on that apprehension, he does not even set forth by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
let alone by means of the Mahāyāna.
But he, Subhūti, who perceives form as merely an unreal construction and merely an illusion, does not apprehend form within form.
He who does not apprehend form within form does not apprehend the view of form within form.
He who does not perceive the view of form in form does not perceive anything in form;
he who does not perceive anything in form perceives everything in form.
For him who, not perceiving anything in form, perceives everything, that [perception] comes to be.
Apprehension is the perfected nature.
Relying upon that apprehension, one sets out by means of the Mahāyāna;
what need is there to mention the Śrāvakayāna or the Pratyekabuddhayāna?
But he, Subhūti, who perceives feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as merely unreal conceptualization and mere delusion, does not perceive consciousness within consciousness.
He who does not perceive consciousness within consciousness does not perceive the view of consciousness within consciousness;
he who does not perceive the view of consciousness within consciousness does not perceive anything at all within consciousness.
He who does not perceive anything in consciousness perceives everything in consciousness.
He who, not perceiving anything in consciousness, perceives everything—that perception of his becomes perfected.
Relying upon that perception, he eventually sets out by means of the Mahāyāna.
How much less, then, could this be achieved by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle?

Subhūti, in regard to form, a bodhisattva’s engagement in verbal expression through adherence to the literal meaning is the manifestation of the view of a self-identity, the manifestation of craving for rebirth, and the manifestation of the pursuit of non-existence; this is the mark of not having fully understood form.

Subhūti, in the same way, a bodhisattva’s engagement in verbal expression through adherence to the literal meaning regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the manifestation of the view of a self-identity, the manifestation of craving for rebirth, and the manifestation of the pursuit of non-existence; this is the sign of not having fully understood consciousness.

Subhūti, in regard to form, a bodhisattva’s non-engagement in verbal expression through adherence to the literal meaning, the non-engagement in the view of a self-identity, the non-engagement in craving for renewed existence,
and the non-engagement in the pursuit of non-existence, is the sign of having fully understood form.

In the same way, Subhūti, when there is no engagement with speech based on attachment to the literal meaning regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, for a bodhisattva, there is no engagement with the view of a self-identity.
The non-occurrence of craving for renewed existence and the non-occurrence of the search for non-existence are the signs of thorough knowledge regarding consciousness.
Subhūti, there are these three seeds of mind for a bodhisattva regarding form, which, when grasped by conditions, lead to purification:
the seed of the mind of resolute conviction, the seed of the mind of world-weariness, and the seed of the mind that is not lost.

Subhūti, there are these three seeds of the mind for a bodhisattva regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, Subhūti, which— when grasped by conditions— conduce to purification:
the seed of the mind of resolute conviction and the seed of the mind of world-weariness.
And the seed of the mind that is non-perishing.
Subhūti, there are these three kinds of mentalities that a bodhisattva should generate regarding form:
a mentality free from attachment, a mentality free from bondage, and a mentality of purification.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva [generates] such a production of thought regarding form...
He perceives non-arising as the great arising; perceiving it thus, he will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, there are these three kinds of minds that a bodhisattva should generate regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: a mind of non-attachment,
a mind of dissociation, and a mind of purification.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva perceives that the production of thought regarding that consciousness is non-production and a great production, perceiving it in this way, he will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva perceives form as existing, as truly existing, or as non-existing, that bodhisattva should be known as one who does not know reality.
Subhūti, it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
If a bodhisattva perceives a bodhisattva as existing by way of such existence or non-existence,
he should be known as a bodhisattva who does not know reality.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva perceives form as non-existent, as not thus existent, and as neither existent nor non-existent, then he should be known as a bodhisattva who knows reality.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva perceives feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as non-existent, as not existing in that way, and as neither existent nor non-existent, he should be known as a bodhisattva who knows reality.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva who desires to settle the mind in form and is resolving upon form finds that mind wavering, fluctuating, and shifting within form, it should be known that this bodhisattva is one whose resolution is difficult.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva desires to settle the mind upon feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and while resolving upon consciousness, that mind wavers, fluctuates, and vacillates within consciousness,
it should be known that this bodhisattva is difficult to bring to firm resolve.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva desires to concentrate the mind upon form, yet while resolving upon that form does not bind, does not fasten, and does not fetter the mind to form, that bodhisattva should be known as one who possesses mastery over his own resolution.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva desires to concentrate the mind upon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and while resolving upon that consciousness, does not bind the mind to consciousness, does not bind it thoroughly, nor does he bind it diversely, that bodhisattva should be known as one who possesses self-resolute confidence. (15)

Subhūti, a bodhisattva who has set out for the full comprehension of form as a dharma without characteristics, for the pacification of suffering, and for the non-exclusive state of nirvāṇa, should be known as one who has practiced correctly.
And a bodhisattva who has thus correctly practiced quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva who has set out for the full comprehension of the dharma of signlessness regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; for the pacification of suffering; and for the non-exclusive state of nirvāṇa, should be known as one who has practiced correctly.
And a bodhisattva who has practiced correctly in this way will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For the sake of fully understanding the absence of characteristics, for the pacification of suffering,
and for the sake of peace that is not one-sided.
The bodhisattva enters [into it]. || 1 ||

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, the phenomenon that is without light in form, yet is universal light, along with its basis and its entry, he swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, the phenomenon that is without light and yet possesses universal light regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— along with its basis and its entry— he quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The phenomenon that is without light and yet is universal light,
and the entry into its basis— this is it.
Having known that, one attains awakening. || 2 ||

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva searches for form within form and does not perceive it, and having rendered form non-manifest and penetrated the equality of the dharma of form, he swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva searches for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and not finding them, does not bring consciousness into appearance and penetrates the equality of the dharma of consciousness,
he quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Having grasped and attained the foremost dharma, he is a being whose mind is without appearance;
he is a master of supernormal knowledge regarding the true nature of phenomena.
The wise one attains awakening. || 3 ||

Subhūti, a bodhisattva who is skilled in the non-existence of form, being endowed with the dissolution of form and remaining immovable within the dharma-realm of form, quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti,
a bodhisattva who is skilled in the non-existence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, being endowed with the dissolution of consciousness...
Being immovable within the realm of consciousness and the dharma-realm, one swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The wise one is skilled in non-existence, endowed with the cultivation [of insight],
and immovable within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
One attains omniscience. || 4 ||
Subhūti, by understanding form as it truly is—as being without meaning, without purpose, yet of great significance—a bodhisattva swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, that there is no meaning, no purpose, yet a great purpose, in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, he quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Whether it be meaningless, harmful,
or of great significance, the perfectly awakened one is indeed the Bodhisattva, even when speaking that which is true.
For he indeed attains awakening.

(18) Subhūti, in regard to form, a bodhisattva, having fully understood them, must avoid five types of passion: passion for discursive thought (*vitarka-rāga*), passion for deliberation (*pratarka-rāga*), passion for conceptual construction (*vikalpa-rāga*), passion, and great passion (*mahā-rāga*).
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva, having fully understood them, must completely avoid five types of passion:
passion for discursive thought, passion for deliberation, passion for conceptualization, passion, and great passion.
Subhūti, having completely abandoned these five types of passion regarding form, a bodhisattva does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of form.
Not apprehending the intrinsic nature of form, he does not apprehend form within form.
Not perceiving form within form,
one perceives form within form.
That very perception of form within form is itself the non-perception of form within form.
By means of that non-apprehension of the apprehension of form, having overcome form in every respect, he sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva has completely abandoned these five attachments regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
Not apprehending the intrinsic nature of consciousness, [he dwells] in consciousness...
One does not apprehend consciousness.
Not apprehending consciousness within consciousness,
one apprehends consciousness within consciousness.
That very perception of consciousness within consciousness is itself the non-perception of consciousness within consciousness.
By means of that non-perception of the perception of consciousness, having overcome consciousness in every respect, one goes forth toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, regarding form, a bodhisattva, having fully understood five types of aversion, should abandon them:

aversion consisting of applied thought and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), aversion consisting of reflection and sustained thought (*pratarka-vicāra*), aversion consisting of conceptualization and sustained thought (*vikalpa-vicāra*), aversion, and great aversion.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva, having fully understood five types of aversion, must abandon them:

aversion consisting of discursive thought and investigation, aversion consisting of reflection and investigation, aversion consisting of conceptualization and investigation, aversion, and great aversion.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva has completely avoided these five aversions regarding form,
he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of form.
Not apprehending the intrinsic nature of form, [he does not apprehend it].
One does not perceive form within form.
Not perceiving form within form, one perceives form within form.
That very perception of form within form—this is [the non-perception].
In form, there is the non-apprehension of form. By that non-apprehension of the apprehension of form, one emerges having overcome form in every respect— that is, for the sake of unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva has avoided these five types of aversion regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
Not apprehending the intrinsic nature of consciousness, he does not apprehend consciousness within consciousness.
Not perceiving consciousness within consciousness, one perceives consciousness within consciousness.
That very perception of consciousness within consciousness is itself the non-perception of consciousness within consciousness.
By means of that non-apprehension of the apprehension of consciousness, having overcome consciousness in every respect, he goes forth toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, regarding form, a bodhisattva, having fully understood them, should avoid five delusions:
the delusion of error, the delusion of the sign of error, the delusion of the sign of non-error, delusion, and great delusion.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva, having fully understood them, must abandon five delusions:
the delusion of error;...
Delusion regarding the cause of error, delusion regarding the cause of non-error, delusion, and great delusion.
Subhūti, having avoided these five delusions regarding form, a bodhisattva does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of form.
Not apprehending the intrinsic nature of form,
he does not apprehend form within form.
Not perceiving form within form, one perceives form within form.
That very perception of form within form is itself the non-perception of form within form.
By means of that non-perception of the perception of form, having overcome form in every respect, one goes forth toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, having avoided these five delusions regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
Not apprehending the intrinsic nature of consciousness, he does not apprehend consciousness within consciousness.
Not apprehending consciousness within consciousness, one apprehends consciousness within consciousness.
That very apprehension of consciousness within consciousness is itself the non-apprehension of consciousness within consciousness.
By means of that non-apprehension of the apprehension of consciousness, having overcome consciousness in every respect, he sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, regarding form, a bodhisattva, having fully understood them, should avoid five types of pride:
the pride of much learning, the pride of exaltation, the pride of overestimation, pride, and great pride.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva, having fully understood five types of pride, must abandon them:
the pride of erudition, the pride of eminence, overweening pride, pride, and great pride.
Subhūti, having avoided these five types of conceit regarding form, a bodhisattva does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of form;
not apprehending the intrinsic nature of form, he...
One does not perceive form in form;
not perceiving form in form,
one perceives form in form.
Whatever apprehension of form there is in form,
that itself is the non-apprehension of form in form; by means of that non-apprehension of the apprehension of form...
Having overcome form in every respect, one goes forth toward that which is unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Subhūti, having avoided these five types of conceit regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
Not apprehending the intrinsic nature of consciousness, he does not apprehend consciousness within consciousness.
Not apprehending consciousness within consciousness, he apprehends consciousness within consciousness.
That very perception of consciousness within consciousness is itself the non-perception of consciousness within consciousness.
By means of that non-perception of the perception of consciousness, having overcome consciousness in every respect, he goes forth toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, regarding form, a bodhisattva, having fully understood them, should avoid five views:
the view of the inversion of intrinsic nature, the view that [things] exist, the view of denial, the view, and the great view.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva, having fully understood them, must abandon five views:
the view of the inversion of intrinsic nature, the view that "it exists," the view of denial, the view, and the great view.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva has completely abandoned these five views regarding form, he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of form;
not apprehending the intrinsic nature of form, [he does not perceive it].
One does not perceive form in form;
not perceiving form in form,
one perceives form in form.
Whatever perception of form there is regarding form, that itself is the non-perception of form regarding form.
By means of that non-perception of the perception of form, one emerges having overcome form in every respect; that is to say, for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva,
having avoided these five views, does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
Not apprehending the intrinsic nature of consciousness, he does not apprehend consciousness within consciousness.
Not apprehending consciousness within consciousness, he apprehends consciousness within consciousness.
That very apprehension of consciousness within consciousness is itself the non-apprehension of consciousness within consciousness.
By means of that non-apprehension of the apprehension of consciousness, having overcome consciousness in every respect, he goes forth toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, regarding form, a bodhisattva, having fully understood them, should avoid five kinds of doubt:
doubt concerning phenomena, doubt concerning the suffering of the realms of existence, doubt concerning nirvāṇa, the Buddha, bodhisattvas, and the Dharma, doubt, and great doubt.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva, having fully understood five types of doubt, must abandon them:
doubt concerning the Dharma; doubt concerning the realms of existence and suffering; doubt concerning nirvāṇa, the Buddha, bodhisattvas, and the Dharma; doubt; and great doubt.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva has avoided these five types of uncertainty regarding form, he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of form.
Not apprehending the intrinsic nature of form, he does not apprehend form within form.
Not apprehending form within form, he apprehends form within form.
Whatever perception of form there is in form, that itself is the non-perception of form in form.
By means of that non-perception of the perception of form, one emerges having overcome form in every respect—that is, for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, having avoided these five doubts regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
Not apprehending the intrinsic nature of consciousness, he does not apprehend consciousness within consciousness.
Not perceiving consciousness within consciousness, one perceives consciousness within consciousness.
That very perception of consciousness within consciousness is itself the non-perception of consciousness within consciousness.
By means of that non-perception of the perception of consciousness, one transcends consciousness in every respect, namely, for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva seeks form, teaches the Dharma regarding form, and purifies the actions of body, speech, and mind with respect to form, he seeks that form according to its literal expression, according to its appearance, and according to its description;
he teaches the Dharma and purifies those actions of body, speech, and mind therein.
A bodhisattva who seeks after form should be known as one who has spoken improper words and actions;
and in that regard, a bodhisattva whose bodily, vocal, and mental actions are impure should be known [as such].

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva seeks form, teaches the Dharma regarding form, and purifies the actions of body, speech, and mind with respect to form, he seeks that form as it is not according to sound, not according to view, and not according to what is proclaimed;
he teaches the Dharma and purifies those actions of body, speech, and mind in that manner.
A bodhisattva who thoroughly investigates form should be known as one who has correctly explained speech and action;
and in that regard, a bodhisattva whose actions of body, speech, and mind are completely pure should be known [as such].

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva investigates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, teaches the Dharma regarding consciousness, and purifies the actions of body, speech, and mind with respect to consciousness,

he investigates that consciousness according to its literal expression, according to how it is seen, and according to how it is described; he teaches the Dharma and purifies those actions of body, speech, and mind.
A bodhisattva who investigates consciousness [in this manner] should be known as one who speaks of improper speech and action;
and in that consciousness, a bodhisattva should be known as one whose actions of body, speech, and mind are impure.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva seeks consciousness, teaches the Dharma regarding consciousness, and purifies the actions of body, speech, and mind within consciousness, he seeks that consciousness not according to sound, not according to view, and not according to what has been proclaimed;
thus he teaches the Dharma and purifies those actions of body, speech, and mind therein.
A bodhisattva who thoroughly investigates consciousness should be known as one who has correctly described speech and action;
and regarding that consciousness—
A bodhisattva whose actions of body, speech, and mind are completely purified should be known as such.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva desires to concentrate the mind upon form and, while resolving upon that form internally, perceives duality within duality— namely, the form to be resolved upon and the form that resolves— it is said that the bodhisattva who instructs another regarding form by teaching the resolution according to the object to be resolved, or the object to be resolved according to the resolution, is one who instructs incorrectly regarding form.
One should know [him] as a bodhisattva.
For what reason? Because,
Subhūti, the form that is the object of resolve does not exist as a distinct characteristic from the form that is the act of resolving.

Subhūti, if the form that is the object of resolve were of a different characteristic from the form that is the resolve itself, then for sentient beings who have various resolves, non-differentiated visions regarding the object of their meditative resolve would not be perceived;
nor would a resolve without an objective support be perceived in dreams and the like.
Furthermore, foolish ordinary persons would perceive form as reality;
nor would the form to be resolved upon conform to a non-conceptual resolve that is established and logical.
For this reason, Subhūti, because beings have various inclinations, diverse views arise regarding the object of their resolve in meditative concentration.
Furthermore, in dreams and other such states, an aspiration (adhimokṣa) without an objective basis is observed.
And ordinary worldlings do not perceive form as it truly is.
Once an non-conceptual aspiration is established and proven, the form that is the object of that aspiration conforms to it.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should view the form that is the object of resolve as having no characteristic distinct from the form of the resolve itself;
the resolve upon form with its signs is not other than that form which has arisen as the object of resolve.
Therefore, an object appears as something other [than it truly is].
Seeing in this way, the bodhisattva eliminates the perception of the form that is the object of resolve.

It occurs to him: "When the form that is the object of resolve exists, the form of resolve is tenable, but not when it does not exist. Having understood this, he perceives the error regarding the form of resolve and eliminates even the perception of the form of resolve.
Having eliminated the perception of duality, he does not apprehend any form at all.
Not apprehending any form, he apprehends the delusion of form.
Apprehending the delusion of form, he apprehends the causal sign of the delusion of form.
Perceiving the cause of delusion regarding form, he accumulates the qualities that are non-delusive with respect to form.
Accumulating the qualities that are non-delusive with respect to form, he accumulates the qualities that are the natural outflow of non-delusion regarding form.
Furthermore, he has already previously accumulated the qualities concerning both delusion and non-delusion regarding form.
Relying upon the dharmas of non-delusion and the dharmas that are the outflow of non-delusion with respect to form, he cultivates all the qualities of a Buddha,
brings sentient beings to maturity,
and purifies the buddha-field.
And he swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who instructs in such a manner is one who instructs correctly.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva desires to concentrate the mind upon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and while resolving that consciousness to be internal, perceives duality within duality— namely, the consciousness to be resolved upon and the consciousness that resolves— it is a case where the bodhisattva instructs regarding consciousness either by teaching the resolution according to the object to be resolved upon, or by teaching the object to be resolved upon according to the resolution. Such a bodhisattva is one who instructs incorrectly regarding consciousness.
It should be understood.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the consciousness of the object of resolution does not have a characteristic distinct from the consciousness of resolution.

If, Subhūti, the consciousness of the object of resolution had a characteristic distinct from the consciousness of resolution, then among beings with diverse inclinations, non-differentiated visions would not be perceived within their common resolution in meditative concentration.
Furthermore, no resolute conviction in the absence of an objective basis would be perceived in dreams and the like;
and ordinary worldlings would become seers of reality within their own consciousness.
Furthermore, once the non-conceptual resolve (*nirvikalpādhimokṣa*) is established and logically proven, the consciousness that resolves upon the object of resolve would not continue to function.
For this reason, Subhūti, because beings with diverse inclinations (*nānādhimukti*) give rise to various divergent views regarding the object of their resolve,
and because a resolve without an objective support (*anālambana-adhimokṣa*) is observed even in dreams and similar states.
Furthermore, foolish ordinary persons do not perceive reality within consciousness.
When there is a firm conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that is established and logical regarding the non-conceptual, the consciousness of the object of conviction follows accordingly.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva [should understand] that the consciousness of the object of conviction does not have a characteristic distinct from the consciousness of the conviction itself.
It should be observed that the conviction of consciousness (*vijñānādhimokṣa*) held by one who possesses views based on signs does not exist elsewhere than in the consciousness as it has arisen;
therefore, an object appears as something other [than that consciousness].
Seeing in this way, the bodhisattva eliminates the perception of the consciousness that is the object of resolve.

It occurs to him: "When there is a consciousness that is the object of resolve, a consciousness of resolve is possible, but not when it is absent. Having understood this, he perceives the error regarding the consciousness of resolve.
He also eliminates the perception of the consciousness of resolute conviction.
Having eliminated the perception of dualistic consciousness, he no longer perceives any consciousness at all.
Not perceiving any consciousness, he perceives delusion within consciousness.
Perceiving the error of consciousness, one perceives the cause of the error of consciousness.
Perceiving the cause of the error of consciousness, one accumulates the non-erroneous factors within consciousness.
Having accumulated the non-erroneous factors within consciousness, one accumulates the factors that are the natural outflow of non-error within consciousness.
Furthermore, he has already previously acquired the qualities of non-delusion regarding consciousness.

Relying upon those qualities of non-delusion in consciousness and the qualities that are the natural outflow of non-delusion, he cultivates all the Buddha-qualities and brings sentient beings to maturity.

He purifies the buddha-field and swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. A bodhisattva who instructs in this manner regarding consciousness should be known as one who instructs correctly.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate five forms of loving-kindness toward form:

loving-kindness that brings about the true Dharma, loving-kindness that brings about worldly happiness, loving-kindness that brings about supramundane happiness, loving-kindness, and great loving-kindness. (31)
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate five kinds of loving-kindness:

loving-kindness that brings about the true Dharma, loving-kindness that brings about worldly happiness, loving-kindness that brings about supramundane happiness, loving-kindness, and great loving-kindness.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate five aspects of compassion regarding form:
the compassion of non-inclusion, the compassion of union, the compassion of non-union, compassion, and great compassion.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate five aspects of compassion:
compassion that does not involve grasping, compassion for those who are joined [to suffering], compassion for those who are not joined [to suffering], compassion, and great compassion.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate five forms of sympathetic joy (*muditā*) regarding form: sympathetic joy consisting of rejoicing in the favor of the outpouring of serene confidence in the true Dharma; sympathetic joy consisting of rejoicing in the favor of the outpouring of worldly happiness; sympathetic joy consisting of rejoicing in the favor of the outpouring of supramundane happiness; sympathetic joy;
and great sympathetic joy.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate five forms of sympathetic joy (*muditā*):

sympathetic joy consisting in rejoicing at the favor of the moistening of serene confidence in the true Dharma; sympathetic joy consisting in rejoicing at the favor of the moistening of worldly happiness; and sympathetic joy consisting in rejoicing at the favor of the moistening of supramundane happiness.
Sympathetic joy and great sympathetic joy.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate five kinds of equanimity regarding form:

equanimity that brings about the absence of defilement through false views; equanimity that brings about the absence of defilement by avoiding all faults; equanimity that brings about the absence of defilement by embracing all virtues; equanimity; and great equanimity.
Subhūti, [a bodhisattva] should [cultivate these] regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

A Mahāsattva should cultivate five kinds of equanimity: equanimity that brings about the absence of defilement through false views; equanimity that brings about the absence of defilement by avoiding all faults; equanimity that brings about the absence of defilement by embracing all virtues; equanimity; and great equanimity.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of generosity within form should cultivate five kinds of giving: the giving of a promise, the giving of material things and the gift of fearlessness, the giving of the practice of the Dharma, the giving of the Dharma itself, and the great giving.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of generosity with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should cultivate five kinds of giving: the gift of promise, the gift of material things and the gift of protection from fear,
the gift of the practice of the Dharma, and the great gift.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of ethical discipline regarding form should cultivate fivefold ethical discipline:

the conventional ethical discipline of undertaking vows, the ethical discipline of meditative restraint, the ethical discipline of untainted restraint, ethical discipline, and great ethical discipline.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of ethical discipline regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should likewise cultivate fivefold ethical discipline.
The morality of undertaking conventional precepts, the morality of restraint through meditative concentration, the morality of untainted restraint, morality, and great morality.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of patience regarding form should cultivate five kinds of patience:
the patience of enduring harm from sentient beings, the patience of accepting suffering, the patience of reflecting on the Dharma, patience, and great patience.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of patience regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should cultivate five forms of patience:
the patience of enduring injury from sentient beings, the patience of accepting suffering, the patience of reflecting on the Dharma, the patience [of non-arising], and great patience.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of vigor regarding form should cultivate five kinds of vigor:
the vigor of mental application for recitation and study, the vigor of completely abandoning all faults, the vigor of fully embracing all virtues, vigor, and great vigor.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of vigor with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should cultivate fivefold vigor:
the vigor of mind for recitation and study, the vigor of avoiding all faults, the vigor of embracing all virtues, vigor, and great vigor.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of meditation regarding form should cultivate five kinds of meditation:
skillful meditation dependent on letters, skillful mundane meditation that is pure and independent of letters and so forth, supramundane skillful meditation, meditation, and great meditation.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of meditation with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should cultivate fivefold meditation:
meditation dependent on syllables; wholesome mundane meditation that is independent of syllables and so forth, which is pure; supramundane wholesome meditation; meditation; and great meditation.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of wisdom should cultivate five aspects of wisdom regarding form:

wisdom based on skillful meditative concentrations that depend on the literal expression; wisdom based on pure mundane meditative concentrations that do not depend on the literal expression; wisdom based on supramundane meditative concentrations; wisdom; and great wisdom.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of wisdom should likewise cultivate these five aspects of wisdom regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Wisdom that relies on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that is skillful yet dependent on the literal expression; wisdom that relies on pure mundane meditative concentration that is independent of the literal expression and so forth; and wisdom that relies on supramundane meditative concentration—Subhūti, this is wisdom, this is great wisdom. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is engaged in attending upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) should attend upon that spiritual friend through five modes of attendance: through the attendance of listening, through the attendance of service, attendance, and following the training, through the attendance of accomplishing the practice, and through attendance and great attendance.

Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is devoted to serving a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) should serve that spiritual friend through five modes of service:

by means of service consisting of hearing [the Dharma], service consisting of attendance and personal care along with compliance with the training, service consisting of the fulfillment of practice, service, and great service.
In this way, by serving a spiritual friend, a bodhisattva mahāsattva grasps the means to liberation,
generates abundant merit,
and swiftly sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. (36)
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the worship of the Tathāgata should worship the Tathāgata with five kinds of worship:
worship consisting of various hymns and offerings, worship consisting of the presentation of gain and honor, worship consisting of the fulfillment of practice, worship, and great worship.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the worship of the Tathāgata should worship the Tathāgata with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness by means of fivefold worship of the Tathāgata:
worship consisting of various hymns and offerings, worship consisting of the presentation of gain and honor, worship consisting of the fulfillment through practice, worship, and great worship.

Thus, for the bodhisattva mahāsattva who is engaged in the worship of the Tathāgata, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas in the infinite and boundless world-systems of the ten directions proclaim his praise;
he receives gain and honor from the world including its gods, humans, and asuras;
and he brings immeasurable sentient beings to spiritual maturity.
He purifies the buddha-field and swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in the perfection of generosity who cultivates generosity with signs does not quickly fulfill the perfection of generosity;
however, by cultivating signless generosity, he quickly fulfills the perfection of generosity.
And how, Subhūti, [does this occur]?
A bodhisattva cultivates giving toward form either with signs or without signs.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, while being intent upon giving toward form, perceives the act of intending, or perceives the gift as an object of intention, or perceives it as having signs, then it should be understood that the bodhisattva is cultivating giving toward form with signs.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva is resolved upon giving in regard to form, one should know that he does not apprehend a gift of resolution, nor a gift consisting of resolution— namely, by way of the non-apprehension of the intrinsic nature of form,
the non-apprehension of its suchness, and the non-apprehension of its primordial nature; thus it should be understood that the bodhisattva cultivates a signless gift in regard to form.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva engaged in the perfection of generosity while focused on feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, if he cultivates generosity with signs, does not quickly fulfill the perfection of generosity;
however, by cultivating signless generosity, he quickly fulfills the perfection of generosity.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva cultivate giving with signs or without signs in relation to consciousness?

If, Subhūti, while a bodhisattva is resolving upon giving in relation to consciousness, he perceives either the act of resolution or the gift itself as having signs, it should be understood that the bodhisattva is cultivating giving with signs in relation to consciousness.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva is intent upon giving while [focused] on consciousness, he does not apprehend a gift of resolve, nor a gift consisting of resolve; that is to say, through the non-apprehension of the intrinsic nature of consciousness, through the non-apprehension of its suchness, and through the non-apprehension of its essential nature.
It should be understood that the bodhisattva cultivates a signless gift within consciousness.
The same should be applied in detail to ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should fully understand the concentration on emptiness regarding form.
And what, Subhūti, is the concentration on emptiness regarding form?

It is, Subhūti, that one-pointedness of mind which takes as its object the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of such existence, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature regarding form; this is the concentration on emptiness regarding form.
And in this way, the bodhisattva should fully understand the concentration on emptiness regarding form.
Subhūti, in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva must fully understand the concentration on emptiness.
And what, Subhūti, is [the concentration on emptiness] in consciousness?

The concentration on emptiness: Subhūti, that one-pointedness of mind which, having taken as its object the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of such existence, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature within consciousness— this is the concentration on emptiness regarding consciousness.
And in this way, the bodhisattva should fully understand the concentration on emptiness regarding consciousness.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva must fully understand the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) regarding form.
And what, Subhūti, is the signless concentration regarding form?

It is that, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva attends to the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of such existence, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) regarding form, [the notion of form] ceases.

Subhūti, that one-pointedness of mind which is devoid of consciousness following the sign of non-existence, devoid of consciousness following the sign of existence, and devoid of consciousness following the signs of both existence and non-existence—
this, with respect to form, is the signless samādhi. And in this way, the signless samādhi regarding form should be fully understood by a bodhisattva.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva must fully comprehend the signless samādhi with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. And what, Subhūti, is the signless samādhi with respect to consciousness?
It is that which, Subhūti, is the bodhisattva’s emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of suchness, and emptiness of intrinsic nature with respect to consciousness.

And for one who attends to it in this way, Subhūti, when the sign has ceased, there is the signless concentration in consciousness— [a state] devoid of consciousness following after the sign of non-existence, devoid of consciousness following after the sign of such existence, and devoid of consciousness following after the signs of both existence and non-existence.
And in this manner, the Bodhisattva should fully understand the signless concentration in consciousness.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva must fully understand the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) regarding form.
And what, Subhūti, is the wishless concentration regarding form?
It is, Subhūti, that which pertains to one who has attained the emptiness and signless concentrations regarding form—the non-existence [of intrinsic nature] in form.

Subhūti, one-pointedness of mind which has as its object the repulsive nature of signs, likewise that which has as its object the repulsive nature of the signs of existence, and that which has as its object the repulsive nature of the signs of both existence and non-existence—this is the wishless concentration regarding form.
And in this way, the wishless concentration regarding form should be fully understood by a bodhisattva.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva must fully understand the concentration of wishlessness regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
And what, Subhūti, is the concentration of wishlessness regarding consciousness?

It is that, Subhūti, which for one who has attained the concentrations of emptiness and signlessness in regard to consciousness, takes as its object the non-existence of signs and that which is contrary to them within consciousness.

Subhūti, that one-pointedness of mind which has as its object the sign of non-existence and is adverse to the sign of existence, and which has as its object the sign of both existence and non-existence and is adverse to them—this is the wishless samādhi regarding consciousness.
And in this way, the wishless samādhi regarding consciousness should be fully understood by a bodhisattva. (41)
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should thoroughly understand impermanence in regard to form through three meanings:
by way of the meaning of non-existence, the meaning of destruction, and the meaning of being with stain and without stain.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva should fully understand impermanence through three meanings:
the meaning of non-existence, the meaning of destruction, and the meaning of being both with and without stain.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should fully understand the nature of suffering in form through three meanings:
by way of the meaning of attachment, the meaning of the threefold characteristic, and the meaning of connection.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva must fully understand their nature as suffering through three meanings:
the meaning of attachment, the meaning of the threefold characteristic, and the meaning of connection.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should thoroughly understand the selflessness of form through three meanings:
by way of the meaning of selflessness due to non-existence, by way of the meaning of selflessness due to being thus, and by way of the meaning of selflessness by nature.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva should thoroughly understand their selflessness through three meanings:
by way of the meaning of selflessness as non-existence, by way of the meaning of selflessness as suchness, and by way of the meaning of selflessness as intrinsic nature.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should thoroughly understand the peace of nirvāṇa regarding form through three meanings:
by way of the meaning of the ultimate peace of non-existence, and by way of the meaning of the peace of suchness.
And by way of the meaning of the peace of natural purity.
Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva should fully understand the peace of nirvāṇa through three meanings:
by way of the meaning of non-existence and ultimate peace.
By way of the pacification of such existence and by way of the pacification of natural purity.

Thus spoke the Blessed One; and the elder Subhūti, filled with joy, as well as those monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The Noble Mother Prajñāpāramitā Entering into Essential Nature in Five Hundred Lines.
